newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Armed gangs spread fear in lawless Albanian south.
newsitem.headline: Armed gangs spread fear in lawless Albanian south.

text.p: Armed youths roaming southern Albania have spread fear in near-deserted towns and villages just four days ahead of a general election, called to try to restore stability in the Balkan nation.
In the rebel-run town of Sarande, the only men on the street without a gun are the local policemen.

Youths waving Kalashnikov rifles through car windows zoom through the central square, taxi drivers prominently display guns and hand grenades, and even a local candidate for Sunday's national election says she is armed.

"I have three Kalashnikovs at home and I usually carry a pistol," Konstandina Bezhani, who is running for the Union of Human Rights party that represents the large ethnic Greek minority in the south, told Reuters.
During the interview, news emerged that Bezhani's father Theodhori had been seized near the lawless town of Gjirokaster, about 60 km (40 miles) to the northeast.

She said she had received a call from men claiming to hold her father who told her to withdraw from the parliamentary race if she wanted to see him again. Theodhori Bezhani was one of five ethnic Greeks arrested for a time in 1994 on suspicion of illegal weapons possession and spying for Greece.

With thousands of weapons looted from army depots now in the hands of criminal gangs and teenagers, more than 1,500 people have been killed since the collapse of a string of dubious pyramid investment schemes earlier this year.
Three of the pyramid funds went bust in the south, swallowing the life savings of most Albanian immigrant workers.
Riots by impoverished investors soon spread further north, forcing President Sali Berisha, head of the right-wing Democratic Party, to call snap elections.

But few will be in Sarande to vote on Sunday, Konstandina Bezhani said. Most people have left to seek work abroad and support their families while others fled to escape the violence that has engulfed their once-tranquil town of 25,000.
Those who stayed behind to protect their homes or older relatives have adjusted to a daily grind defined by guns and have to rely on help from abroad to buy basic necessities.
Every day, a small ferry boat delivers food and other supplies from the nearby Greek island of Corfu, but prices have shot up 400 percent since March, according to locals.
"My pension is $25 a month. If my children were not working in Athens, my wife and I would starve," said Andrea Tsaka, a retired ethnic Greek school teacher.

He said that although the Communists, who ruled Albania for 45 years until 1990, sent him to a forced-labour prison for teaching Greek in the 1960s, nothing has scared him as much as the anarchy that has engulfed the region.
"This town has been taken over by thugs who terrorise people. They break into houses wearing masks and wreck everything. They hit the men and rape the women," Tsaka said.

Bezhani is forced to travel to her nearby electoral district in a convoy of three jeeps, escorted by eight armed bodyguards. "These kids have nothing, no money, no work. They just want a better future," she said.

The young men, who blame Berisha for the crash of the pyramid funds, say they will not put down their weapons before he steps down. "When Berisha is gone we will shoot all our bullets in the air and put our guns away for good," said Arben Deneko, 25.
But older people say their sons are out of control and pin their hopes on help from the West, saying only foreign military intervention could restore order in the chaotic south.
"Look at that policeman strolling down the street," said 60-year-old Hujredin Cakeri. "He puts on his uniform but he carries no gun. What can he do against these young men?"
